My settings of encounter rate, detection function and cluster size were all at stratum level.

My question is if I can and how to apply different truncations to different strata.

Thanks,
Eugene

I've not encountered a situation in which I would have wanted stratum-specific truncation distances.

Dear Eric,

Thank you for your clear advice.

I am putting my hands on past data-sets which have been analysed and reported by another consultant, both the data-set and reports were on annual base. What I have are the raw data of sighting effort and records, as well as the results in report which presented the density, abundance and CV for each stratum. What I don't have is the context of DISTANCE analysis.

The findings (densities and CVs) in report were presented for each stratum, and the overall abundance was given as summation of abundance of all strata (geographic areas) which did not come with associated CV and range.

I reckon, after some preliminary runs on my own, the data for each stratum have been treated (truncated) independently in the past analyses to obtain the detection functions and subsequent density estimates. The rationale is not clear to me, but possibly be due to the variation in sightability between geographic areas for this near-shore species.

Under this preset situation, I am seeking if I can obtain a sound overall abundance estimate when each stratum has been truncated differently. I would try out the stratum-specific truncations before entering the program and see if there is meaningful difference in the overall density estimates.

Much appreciate your enlightenment.

Best,
Eugene

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Using the MRDS engine in Distance 6, I come out with a single observer estimate with a cv of 0.35. Using the same data in an independent observer with point independence analysis, and utilizing the same Distance Sampling model as in the single observer analysis, I realize a corrected estimate with a cv of 0.34. The estimate of p(0) has a cv of 0.11.

This seems counter-intuitive to me. Can the corrected estimate have a lower overall variance than the single observer estimate? I have not seen this in any other analysis I have done.

Thanks,

Daniel Pike.

messages.body_plain:
Daniel, I can see this might be possible if g(0) is positively correlated with animal density.  When density is higher, observer concentration might be better.  Then when encounter rate is high, g(0) is high, and their ratio will then be less variable than encounter rate on its own, with g(0) assumed to be one.  Positive correlation between g(0) and f(0) would have a similar effect.  If some observers concentrate their search effort near the line, they would have a larger g(0) and larger f(0) (i.e. the det fn falls away more quickly with distance from the line) than for observers who concentrate more effort away from the line.

Steve Buckland

messages.body_plain:
Anne

Welcome to this beautiful world.

The address "dist...@st-andrews.ac.uk" is usually used for programme bugs and installation hassles.  We maintain a Google groups email list (that I have copied on this email).  The purpose of the email list is to address methodological questions such as yours.  The reason for the email list is that this list is searchable by anyone in the future looking for an answer to a related question.

Now, about your question of including a slope covariate.  I presume you mean adding a slope covariate to the detection function.  This is described and an example provided in Chapter 5 of our online distance sampling course.  There are two video lectures on the subject, plus an exercise with four example data sets and a narrated video solution.  All can be explored free of charge at

https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/syllabus/Chapter5/

To compare between models with and without the slope covariate; I'd be reluctant to compare the estimates themselves and base my inference regarding the utility of the slope covariate on model selection tools, namely AIC.  The model with the smallest AIC would be the model on which I would base my inference (unless I had knowledge to the contrary).

I hope I have interpreted your question correctly; if not, please ask again, using the Google group list.

Hi Antonella, hi listfolk,

It's likely the case that this covariate "doesn't matter" in the model,
so there's nothing that you can really do to "make" it significant (and
in fact this is not a good idea in general).

"Doesn't matter" probably deserves some unpacking here -- likely it's
the case that there is simply not enough signal in the data for the
covariate to explain any of the variation. This can happen if (for your
example, presumably geographical coordinates) there isn't any variation
in, say, Easting. In some cases one might be better off estimating
abundance or density using design-based methods (Horvitz-Thompson
estimation).

Hope this helps,

Sara

Very impressive persistence on your part to get your study area into Distance.  Congratulations.

Now that you've gotten your shapefile into Distance and built your coverage grid; you are able to prepare your design.  Let me proceed through your questions.

- Effort allocation for equal angle design: often investigators have an idea of the amount of ship time or fuel they have in their budget.  Time or fuel can be converted to distances, which can be entered as "available effort."

- effort determined by sampler angle: the smaller the angle the closer together will be the legs of the zigzag.  the 'appropriate' angle would be determined by trial and error

- equal spaced zigzag spacing: determined by trial and error again; closer spacing of turnaround points will result in greater amount of effort

http://distancesampling.org/downloads/distancebook1993/chapter7.pdf  Proportion of study area sampled is not a design criterion.  Quite good results can be accomplished with proportion of study area >1% under many circumstance.

messages.subject_clean: Multi-species, multi-site density estimates, accounting for effort
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am learning how to use the Distance package in R, having for many years used Distance for Windows.

The kind of analysis I am trying to do involves generating separate density estimates for each species at each point count location. I want to do this in order to be able to carry out multivariate analyses to assess similarity in species assemblages between points. It doesn't matter to me that reliability in individual point estimates will be low - the overall patterns (in terms of how points cluster in ordination space in relation to variables such as habitat) are still useful.

I have attached an example dataset comprising 921 observations of 91 species detected at 79 points. The maximum distance within which birds were recorded was 100m. I am ignoring the influence of habitat on location, for the moment, but have assigned each species to one of 13 'detection groups'. Members of each group are assumed to be similarly detectable to one another. With the exception of one group (Hirundines and Swifts, DG13, with only 14 observations) all groups are more or less large enough to based a detection function on the distribution of detection distances.

My first question is whether I could or should use detection group as a co-variate, or whether I should more simply (but also more faffily) apply the ds function separately on each detection group, simply subsetting the whole dataset by detection group? The latter approach is equivalent to the one I have taken previously using the Distance programme. As far as I can see, applying ds separately, without co-variates, to each group has two possible benefits. Firstly, some of the error messages my tests have generated suggest that analyses without co-variates are a little more robust and less inclined to generate errors and warnings. Secondly, if detection distance distributions vary sufficiently between different groups of birds, this may justify applying different key and adjustment functions to model detectability in different detection groups. I'm not sure if this would be possible using a co-variate approach.

My second question relates to generating estimates for each species, at each point. In the Windows programme, I used to create a variable by concatenating (or pasting) species and site names in the following form "Species_Site", and then assigning this variable as a stratum, and specifying stratum as the appropriate level of resolution for density estimates in the Model Definition dialogue. However, the closest I have found to this in the ds function is the Region.Label variable. Is it possible to use this in a similar way?

Finally, my last question is about how to ensure that densities are calculated correctly, taking into account all points where a species wasn't seen, as well as those points where it was. Am I right in thinking that, if I population the Region.Label variable with "Species_Site" (where Site=Point), then I should ensure that a 'blank' entry for every possible unique combination of Species and Site should be included in the dataset to which ds is applied? With 91 species and 79 points, the number of possible unique species-points combinations is 7189. So far, I haven't been able to take this approach successfully. If, as I have read in other posts is the correct approach, I set the distance variable to NA for these records (as in the code below), then I get an error message saying "Error in create.bins(data, cutpoints) : Some distances are NA, can't create bins."

Many thanks for any help you can give!

Best wishes,

Mark

EXAMPLE CODE

messages.body_plain:
Mauro

I needed to create a dataset on which to demonstrate my solution, I used a sample dataset associated with the Buckland et al(2015) book, found here https://synergy.st-andrews.ac.uk/ds-manda/  I've used line transect data of a multi-species bird survey.  Much of the code below simply organises the data, taking account of the fact that not all species are seen on all transects.

The loop at the very bottom for(species in c(("r", "c", "w")) {  loops through three species and does the following:
- fits multiple detection functions to each species,
- chooses the best model based on AIC,
- plots the resulting detection function,
- extracts the point estimate of density and SE for each species
- adds those estimates to the plot title

I used par(mfrow=c(2,2)) to make multiple plots within a single window as you requested.

## ---- startup, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE------------------------------
library(Distance)
library(knitr)

## ---- read-data----------------------------------------------------------
birds.line <- read.csv("https://synergy.st-andrews.ac.uk/ds-manda/files/2016/11/montrave-line.csv")

## ---- transforms---------------------------------------------------------
birds.line$Effort <- birds.line$Effort * birds.line$repeats

augment.empty.transects <- function(birds.line, species) {
  #  Purpose: find transects on which species not detected
  #           adjust data file accordingly such that effort is correct
  #  Input: raw data file, species on which to subset data
  #  Output: data frame ready to have detection function fitted (with correct effort)
  #  Rexstad August 2018

  num.transects <- length(unique(birds.line$Sample.Label))
  holes <- which(as.matrix(table(birds.line$species, birds.line$Sample.Label))==0,
                 arr.ind = TRUE)  # row & col of transects without spec detect
  if (length(holes[rownames(holes)==species])==0) {    # species detected on all transects
    species.detects <- birds.line[birds.line$species==species, ]
  } else {
    alltranlen <- vector(mode="numeric", length=num.transects)
    for (i in 1:num.transects) alltranlen[i] <- birds.line$Effort[birds.line$Sample.Label==i][1]
    empty.transects <- NULL
    for (i in 1:length(holes[rownames(holes)==species,2])) {
      empty.label <- holes[rownames(holes)==species,2][i]
      empty.length <- alltranlen[holes[rownames(holes)==species,2]][i]
      empty.record <- cbind(birds.line[1,1:3], empty.label, empty.length)
      empty.transects <- rbind(empty.transects, empty.record)
    }
    empty.transects[ ,c("a", "b", "c")] <- NA
    names(empty.transects) <- names(birds.line)

    species.detects <- birds.line[birds.line$species==species, ]
    species.detects <- rbind(species.detects, empty.transects)
    species.detects <- species.detects[order(species.detects$Sample.Label), ]
  }
  return(species.detects)
}

##################################################################

## ---- models, message=FALSE----------------------------------------------

fit.hn.uni.haz <- function(data, trunc, print=TRUE) {
  #  Purpose:  fit three key functions to transect data, perform model selection
  #            print model selection table
  #  Input: data to analyse, truncation distance, print model selection table
  #  Output: fitted model object (class `dsmodel`)
  #  Rexstad August 2018
  hn.herm <- ds(data, truncation=trunc, transect="line",
                      key="hn", adjustment="herm", convert.units=.1)
  uni.cos <- ds(data, truncation=trunc, transect="line",
                      key="unif", adjustment="cos", convert.units=.1)
  haz.simp <- ds(data, truncation=trunc, transect="line",
                      key="hr", adjustment="poly", convert.units=.1)
  mods <- summarize_ds_models(hn.herm, uni.cos, haz.simp, output="plain")
  if(print) print(knitr::kable(mods))
  names(mods) <- c("mod","key","form","fit","pa","sepa","daic")
  if(mods[1,1]=="hn.herm") {
    result <- hn.herm
  } else {
    if(mods[1,1]=="uni.cos") {
    result <- uni.cos
  } else {
    result <- haz.simp
  }
  }
  return(result)
}

par(mfrow=c(2,2))
for(species in c("r", "c", "w")) {
  best.model <- fit.hn.uni.haz(augment.empty.transects(birds.line, species), 100) # fits 3 key fns, returns 'best'
  plot(best.model, main=paste("Montrave lines, species ", species,
       "\nD-hat=", round(best.model$dht$individuals$D$Estimate,4),
       "SE=", round(best.model$dht$individuals$D$se, 4)))
}

Dear Sara,

Further to Eric's response, I have had a quick look at your project and E-mail again.

While it is not best practise to generate your survey based on a desired coverage probability it is indeed an option offered for the adjusted angle design so I will explain what was going wrong for you.

You stated in your E-mail that you do not have a maximum width for your observations so I see in your project that you left the sampler width as the default of 1m. However, Distance uses the sampler width to calculate the coverage - it needs to calculate the area covered by the samplers and then divide this by the total area of the study region. This is why Distance was struggling to generate your adjusted angle design... it would have needed to generate many many many of these extremely thin transects in order to achieve the 5% coverage that you requested and ends up hanging.

When you are assessing coverage (usually for the purposes of assessing whether you have uniform coverage probability) it is a good idea to look at past surveys and get an idea about a realistic truncation distance for the sampler width.

As per Eric's recommendation I would stick with the equal spaced zigzag design, I have also noticed that the adjusted angle is a bit temperamental when generating the transects. If you are concerned about the effects of the uneven coverage please take advantage of the simulation engine to reassure yourself that this design should only introduce minimal amounts of bias (if indeed any) to the density/abundance estimates. The exact effects will depend on your particular situation and this is exactly what the simulation engine was designed to assess.

I also note that you are using an older version of Distance so I would also recommend for using the simulation engine that you download Distance 7.2.

messages.body_plain:
Hello Rachel

Don't interpret the bars of the combined detection function/data histogram figure as a probability; that definition applies to the curve, not the bars.  You don't say if these are line or point transects; the default for the ds() function is line transects, so I'll work on that assumption.  You also do not mention your species, but I'm guessing that because they fly and because your data are truncated at 5 metres, they might be insects.

Now about the lack of fit.  Indeed, your data are unlikely to fit the half normal function depicted there.  However, you'll likely need to look more finely at the histogram (rather than cutpoints at 0.5, you might want cutpoints at 0.1 units for the first 0.5, then 0.25 between 0.5 and 1.5, ...)  This will give you a better appreciation for the shape of your histogram.

However, I note from your 9 detection data provided that the resolution of the measurements seem to be 0.5 units--so a finer histogram might not tell you much more than the histogram you already have.  Snooping further into your data I see "behaviour" of flying/sitting; and that 8 of the 9 detections are with behaviour=flying.  One interpretation of this is that your objects are moving (flying) for the most part and that you (observer=RB) watch them and as they fly they eventually cross the transect, and you record a distance of 0.  That leads to a preponderance of 0's in your data, and you end up with the data you show with a spike in the first histogram bin.  As you note, data such as these are very difficult to fit.

You might want to consult section 10.6 of Buckland et al. (2015) where there is a short section of analysis of butterfly data.   Hope that is of some use to you.

Hi Rachael,

Two other situations that could give rise to a detection probability like this is if:
1. detection probability varies with habitat or detection method, and this in turn varies with distance. For example, if you are surveying butterflies in tall grasses, you might disturb the ones straight in front of you (accounting for their much greater visibility) but the ones immediately to the side might stay put and so you would only see a few of them. Similar to Eric's observation, but this issue would still apply even if you recorded butterflies as you are supposed to (i.e. where you first detect them). The distance assumption that is being transgressed here is, I think, that the observer doesn't affect the behaviour or distribution of the study subject.
2. the butterflies themselves might be non-uniformly distributed so that there are more along your line than in the rest of the habitat. For example, if you were walking along a narrow earthen path, many butterflies might be sunning themselves on it. Most of your observations seem to be flying, as Eric pointed out, but perhaps you record them in the mode of behaviour that you first spot them, and you didn't see them before they flew? If so then you should probably be recording the mode of behaviour that you can infer was happening before the butterfly detected you (so that the assumption that what you are recording isn't influenced by your own actions can hold). However, the non-uniform distribution of butterflies on the path could be a more intractable problem, I think.

Cheers,

Mark
